title: How Argentina uses stablecoins, in 5 charts
gist: Argentine crypto usage is overwhelmingly a dollar-savings behavior — 94% of peso crypto trading goes to stablecoins, the highest share of any major currency Artemis tracks — and although inflation collapsed from 25.5% to 2.1% monthly and dollar purchase restrictions were lifted in April 2025, stablecoin payroll usage leveled off rather than disappearing and Lemon wallet downloads kept rising every quarter. The author's read: stablecoins in Argentina are converting from a crisis hedge into a durable habit.

insights.claim: Roughly 1 in 5 people in Argentina use crypto, one of the highest adoption rates in Latin America.
insights.speaker: Alejandro Flores
insights.so_what: Argentina is the highest-signal live testbed for stablecoin product-market fit; treat its usage curves as a leading indicator for other high-inflation, capital-controlled markets.
insights.quote: where 1 in 5 people use crypto, one of the highest rates in Latin America
insights.locator: Where in the world are people using crypto

insights.claim: Downloads of Argentina's 15 leading crypto apps rose 93% in 2024, nearly doubling year over year.
insights.speaker: Alejandro Flores
insights.so_what: App-download velocity is a cheap, high-frequency proxy for stablecoin demand shocks — worth tracking alongside FX spreads for consumer fintech and wallet exposure.
insights.quote: Downloads of Argentina’s 15 leading crypto apps nearly doubled in 2024, rising 93% from the previous year.

insights.claim: Argentina's dollar preference predates crypto: in 2001–2002 the government froze bank deposits and forcibly converted dollar-denominated deposits and loans into pesos via Decree 214/2002.
insights.speaker: Alejandro Flores
insights.so_what: Stablecoin demand here is rooted in institutional distrust, not novelty — meaning it is far stickier than adoption driven by yield or speculation.
insights.locator: Argentina’s preference for dollars predates crypto.

insights.claim: After Argentina's dollar peg ended, the exchange rate fell from one peso per dollar to nearly four, wiping out roughly three-quarters of the peso's dollar value and entrenching the habit of holding physical dollars outside the banking system.
insights.speaker: Alejandro Flores
insights.so_what: The addressable market for stablecoins is the existing mattress-dollar stock, not just new savings flow — a much larger pool than transaction volume implies.
insights.quote: reinforced the habit of keeping savings in physical dollars outside the banking system — think bills under mattresses or in safe-deposit boxes

insights.claim: Stablecoin uptake in Argentina accelerated only after the government reintroduced currency controls in 2019, capping individuals at $200 in official dollar purchases per month with eligibility rules that excluded many people entirely.
insights.speaker: Alejandro Flores
insights.so_what: Capital-control announcements in any emerging market are a tradeable catalyst for stablecoin volume and local wallet growth.
insights.locator: Stablecoins started to pick up steam

insights.claim: Argentine year-over-year inflation reached 289% in April 2024, and over that same period the share of Argentina-based contractors receiving pay in USDC rose.
insights.speaker: Alejandro Flores
insights.so_what: Payroll is the highest-value stablecoin use case because it converts a one-time hedge into recurring, automated inflows — watch payroll-rail share as the key stablecoin durability metric.

insights.claim: The payroll evidence comes from Deel, an a16z portfolio company that runs payroll in more than 160 countries, used as an indicator of the monthly share of Argentina-based contractors paid in USDC.
insights.speaker: Alejandro Flores
insights.so_what: The dataset is proprietary to a single portfolio company and self-selected toward remote-work contractors — discount it as a proxy for the whole population, and note the disclosed conflict of interest.
insights.quote: The above data comes from a16z portfolio company Deel, which helps run payroll in more than 160 countries.
insights.locator: The above data comes from a16z portfolio company Deel

insights.claim: Indexed to January 2024, Argentine inflation and the USDC contractor-pay share initially moved together, then both declined; as of July 2026 both sat at about a fifth of their respective peaks.
insights.speaker: Alejandro Flores
insights.so_what: Stablecoin payroll adoption is still substantially inflation-beta, not fully decoupled — an 80% drawdown from peak is the honest counterweight to the habit thesis.
insights.quote: As of July 2026, both were holding at about a fifth of their respective peaks.
insights.locator: Since the two metrics are indexed to January 2024

themes.theme: Crypto as a dollar proxy, not speculation

insights.claim: 94% of peso-denominated crypto trading goes into stablecoins — the highest stablecoin share of any major currency Artemis tracks.
insights.speaker: Alejandro Flores
insights.so_what: Argentine crypto flow is essentially FX demand, not risk appetite — do not model this volume as beta to BTC or altcoin cycles.
insights.quote: 94% of peso crypto trading goes to stablecoins — the highest stablecoin share of any major currency Artemis tracks.

insights.claim: In Argentina, buying crypto with pesos functions as buying dollars, making local exchange volume a proxy for unmet FX demand rather than for speculative trading interest.
insights.speaker: Alejandro Flores
insights.so_what: A reusable lens for screening emerging markets: where the stablecoin share of local-currency crypto volume is extreme, the driver is FX repression, and policy liberalization is the main downside risk.

themes.theme: The crypto-dollar premium and its collapse

insights.claim: For several years the crypto dollar in Argentina cost materially more than a dollar bought at the official exchange rate, and by 2023 capital controls pushed the gap between official and parallel rates above 100%.
insights.speaker: Alejandro Flores
insights.so_what: Users paid a >100% premium for 24/7, control-free dollar access — a hard read on willingness-to-pay for censorship-resistant FX that prices the value of the rail itself.
insights.quote: pushed the gap between the official and parallel exchange rates above 100%

insights.claim: After Argentina lifted most restrictions on individuals buying dollars in April 2025, official and parallel rates largely converged, and as of August 28, 2026 a digital dollar costs only about 4% more than one bought through the official market.
insights.speaker: Alejandro Flores
insights.so_what: The arbitrage-driven margin in Argentine stablecoin distribution has compressed from triple digits to ~4%; local exchange and wallet business models must now monetize convenience and volume, not spread.
insights.quote: As of August 28, 2026, a digital dollar costs about 4% more than one bought through the official market.

insights.claim: The conditions that originally drove Argentines to stablecoins — high inflation and inaccessible official dollars — have largely eased, which would normally predict usage fading, but usage has not faded.
insights.speaker: Alejandro Flores
insights.so_what: If stablecoin demand survives macro normalization, the bear case that stablecoins are purely a distress product weakens materially for the whole sector.
insights.quote: You’d expect usage to fade with them. But it hasn’t.
insights.locator: The economic crisis in Argentina seems to be cooling

insights.claim: Downloads of Lemon, one of Argentina's largest crypto wallets, climbed every quarter even as monthly inflation fell from 25.5% to 2.1%.
insights.speaker: Alejandro Flores
insights.so_what: Quarter-over-quarter wallet download growth through a disinflation of that magnitude is the single cleanest evidence of demand decoupling from macro distress — the metric to keep monitoring.
insights.quote: downloads of Lemon, one of Argentina’s largest crypto wallets, climbed every quarter, even as monthly inflation fell from 25.5% to 2.1%
insights.locator: Paycheck usage leveled off instead of disappearing.

insights.claim: Stablecoins in Argentina may be transitioning from an inflation hedge into an ordinary financial habit, implying a structurally higher usage floor even in benign macro conditions.
insights.speaker: Alejandro Flores
insights.so_what: The investable question is the size of that floor: a habit-driven base means recurring transaction revenue for wallets and issuers rather than crisis-cyclical spikes.
insights.quote: Stablecoins may no longer be just a hedge against inflation for Argentines — they could be becoming a habit.
insights.locator: Stablecoins may no longer be just a hedge
